newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ex-finmin sees free-market tide rising.
newsitem.headline: French ex-finmin sees free-market tide rising.

text.p: Alain Madelin, a strongly free-market ex-finance minister ousted by Prime Minister Alain Juppe, said on Monday the calling of an early election should allow France take a more 'liberal', or free-market, tack.

Madelin, pushed out by Juppe after just four months in the finance job following elections in mid-1995 after angering trade unions, is seen by some as a possible alternative once again, to current Finance Minister Jean Arthuis.
Jean Arthuis is seen as a belt-tightener, a staunch advocate of financial rigour and austerity, while Madelin is a fiery proponent of tax cuts and a more hands-off approach to the economy.

"What I didn't want was a policy of rigour but here we're talking about a policy of vigour," Madelin said on TF1 television after President Jacques Chirac announced he was dissolving parliament and calling an election on May 25 and June 1, nine months ahead of the normal election deadline.
"If it's a policy of 'liberal' rigour, I would clearly support it," he said when asked if he would be ready to take his old job back.
"It's a choice of comon sense, a modern choice, one which Christian Democrats have made, and Social Democrats and I would even add, ironically, the Labour Party in Great Britain," he said.
"There's a new train of world growth starting to roll. Are we going to stay behind on the platform or jump onto the train. That's what's at stake in this election," he said.
Also appearing on France 2 state television, Madelin said:
"I think this election will allow us to make a big leap. It will allow the start of the modernisation this country needs.
He also said European monetary union was crucial to France.
"I know one thing. The euro (single currency) is a chance for France and for Europe," he said.
"In any case, I know a bit of vigour will be much better than rigour," he added.

A presidential source said, nevertheless, Chirac's decision to seek a new five-year mandate for parliament was designed to win backing for values which were neither those of the extreme right, nor the "laisser-faire, laisser aller" dear to the "ultraliberals", nor the "archaic solutions" of those who always want more from the state and through taxes.
